title: Evidence profile
subtitle: Four separate questions. Not a score.
why: We never add these up. A compound can have a large animal literature from one laboratory and no human data at all — that is a specific situation, and a single number would hide it.
whyFold: Why these grades: the reason for each step

human_clinical.name: Human clinical evidence
human_clinical.question: How far has it been tested in people?

explain.case-reports: Only individual cases or small uncontrolled series. These can raise questions; they cannot answer them.
explain.phase-1: Small studies, usually in healthy volunteers, mainly about safety and how the body handles the compound.
explain.phase-2: Studies in patients to find doses and look for early signs of effect, usually with a control group.
explain.phase-3: Large randomised controlled trials designed to test whether it works and how often harm occurs.
explain.authorised: A medicines regulator has reviewed the full data and authorised it for specific uses.

preclinical_volume.name: Preclinical volume
preclinical_volume.question: How much laboratory and animal research exists?

explain.minimal: Fewer than about 10 published primary studies in cells or animals.
explain.extensive: More than about 50 published primary studies.

independence.name: Source independence
independence.question: How many independent groups produced it?

explain.single-group-dominant: Most primary studies come from one research group. Their errors, if any, are repeated rather than caught.
explain.few-groups: Two to four groups produced most of the work.
explain.broadly-replicated: Many independent groups, and key findings have been reproduced.

safety.name: Safety characterisation
safety.question: How well do we know the harms in humans?

explain.uncharacterised: No systematic human safety data. Absence of reported harm is not evidence of safety.
explain.partial: Some human exposure data, short-term or small. Rare and long-term harms are unknown.
explain.well-characterised: Large trials plus ongoing post-marketing surveillance. Rare harms are still being learned.

hypothesis.long: Proposed, not demonstrated in any experiment

in-vitro.long: Shown in cells or tissue in the laboratory

human-limited.long: Seen in humans in case reports or small uncontrolled studies

established.long: Established in large trials and authorised use

in-vitro.long: Demonstrated in cells or tissue in the laboratory

matrix.caption: Evidence profiles of all compounds on this site
matrix.note: Sorting arranges compounds by one axis at a time. It does not rank them: the axes are deliberately not combined.
